units: the young deer is born as the cold season ends
at birth it wears a coat covered with spots
through its first weeks it stays motionless in the vegetation
its pale fur makes it hard to tell apart from the ground
its mother moves off to feed and comes back to nurse it
this distance keeps scent from gathering around the hiding place
once its legs grow firm it follows its mother along the trails
the spots fade when the warmth returns
before the next cold season it joins a group of its own kind
text: The cold season loosens its grip, and the fawn arrives in a clearing, too weak to trail its mother more than a few steps. For weeks it lies where the tall grass conceals it, chin flat, ears low, motionless even when a shadow crosses. Its dappled coat borrows the color of dry leaves, so the eye slides past it. The doe drifts off to graze and returns at regular intervals to nurse, and her absence keeps scent from gathering around the hiding place. Once the legs firm up, the young animal finally walks behind her and learns which trails carry the least risk. Warm weather arrives, the spots fade, the coat darkens. Soon it grazes alone, choosing tender shoots by instinct. Before the cold circles back, it falls in with a herd and follows it toward the sheltered slopes. The clearing means nothing to it now.

units: the mare had been limping since the day before
the assistant first blamed the trouble on a simple knock
a stone had in fact wedged itself under the animal's foot
this stone crushed the tissue at every step
without quick action a pocket of pus would have formed
the caregiver pared out the cavity and protected the wound
the animal was moved onto soft ground that cushions its weight
the neglected state of its mane revealed poor upkeep
the team now checks the feet before every outing
text: The mare had been limping since the previous day, and the stable assistant put it down to a bruise. The examination told another story. A sharp stone had wedged itself between the frog and the wall of the hoof, and it crushed the tissue with every step the animal took. Left in place, that pressure would have driven a deep inflammation and then a pocket of pus that drains badly. So the practitioner pared out the cavity, disinfected the wound, and packed it under a thick dressing held by adhesive tape. Since the mare tolerated confinement poorly, she went into a sandy paddock whose loose footing cushioned her weight. Her tangled mane, a sign of grooming let slide, pushed the team to rethink its routine. Weeks later the gait had evened out, and a hoof check now comes before every outing.

units: a claw left to grow too long ends up breaking the skin under the paw
one must pick a moment when the animal is dozing
press the base of the toe until the claw slides out
a colored zone marks where the blood vessels run
the cut must stop short of that zone
going past that limit brings on bleeding
a tool with a curved blade serves better than an ordinary clipper
it is advised to interrupt the session if the animal stiffens
a treat makes every subsequent session easier
text: A claw left to grow too long presses against the pad beneath it and eventually breaks that soft skin. The procedure below corrects the trouble without alarming the cat. Choose a quiet moment, some while after a meal, when the animal lies dozing across a lap. Take one paw gently, press the base of the toe until the claw slides out of its sheath, then locate the pink zone where the blood vessels run through it. The cut must stop well short of that mark; beyond it, bleeding follows immediately, and the pain is considerable. A tool with a curved blade serves far better than an ordinary clipper, whose jaws crush the horn instead of severing it cleanly. Should the animal stiffen, interrupt the session and resume the following day, one paw at a time. A treat afterward makes every subsequent session easier.

units: two neighboring shelters take in abandoned animals
the first gives every resident a pen of its own
the second settles compatible animals into small groups
keeping them apart slows the spread of disease
grouping them cuts down the habits that boredom brings on
adoptions close faster in the shelter that groups its animals
fights, on the other hand, break out more often there
both teams keep the same health record
they send animals to each other as spaces open up
text: Two shelters on either side of a valley take in the animals that the region abandons, and the two of them run on opposite ideas. The first gives every resident a pen of its own. A keeper defends the choice on the grounds of contagion: mange travels slowly when no muzzle ever touches another. The second reads temperaments and settles the compatible ones into small groups, and its director reports a sharp drop in compulsive licking and in the barking that plain boredom brings on. The adoption records bear the difference out. Animals leave faster from the group shelter, where visitors get to watch them interact. Fights break out more often there, and a bitten resident has to be pulled aside on the spot. Both teams keep the same health record, and each one sends animals over to the other as soon as a space opens up.

units: the farmyard belongs to an uncle of the speaker
the rooster carries a red growth on top of its head
a hard spike stands out behind each of its legs
the hens roll around in the dry dust
the ducks have a shallow pond of their own
the geese announce visitors with their cries
a cat sleeps on the woodpile
the uncle hands out grain before nightfall
text: You really ought to see my uncle's farmyard, the whole thing is a spectacle. The rooster runs the place: that red comb goes straight up the second the gate swings open, and the spur behind each leg makes him worth avoiding. The hens spend entire afternoons rolling around in the dry dust, feathers puffed right out, and they come up gray from beak to foot. Down the slope a little, the ducks have a shallow pond of their own that they empty and refill all day long with those flat bills. The geese you hear long before you ever see them, and the moment a car turns onto the lane they start hollering together. Up on the woodpile, an orange cat sleeps straight through the racket. And my uncle comes by with his bucket of grain before dark, the same hour every evening, and the whole yard settles.

units: the first animal collections were there to dazzle the visitor
the animals were shut behind narrow bars
wider cages came later and echoed the original habitats
the parks then set out to breed threatened species
releases back into the wild were attempted
captivity weakens the habits that keep an animal alive
the writer holds that protecting wild land should come first
he grants that a few species hang on only under human watch
text: Once, a collection of animals was there for one purpose, to dazzle the visitor. A big cat behind narrow bars stood for power, and nobody stopped to ask what those bars did to it. Wider cages came later, planted with trees and dug out with pools, meant to echo the habitats the animals had come from. Then the parks claimed a purpose of another order: breed the rare species, keep the bloodlines on paper, send captive-born animals back out to the wild. That last step deserves a hard look. A predator fed at a fixed hour loses the habits that keep it alive, and its release fails far more often than it works. Those budgets would do more for the land itself, for wooded corridors, for rivers freed of their weirs. Still, a handful of species now hang on nowhere but under human watch, and pretending otherwise helps nothing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the trainer grew up on a farm far from any neighbor
an accident took her father's sight
she then taught a dog to guide her father
that success drew other requests
she converted a barn into a training floor
she picks her puppies for their calm in the face of noise
she rejects anything built on fear
her former pupils still come back to ask for her advice
text: The trainer grew up on a farm far from any neighbor, among plow horses and herding dogs. When a farm machine took her father's sight, she set about teaching a young bitch to walk him from the house down to the barn. The dog learned to slow at the steps and to press her muzzle into his hand before every obstacle. Word spread, and families began knocking at the farm door. Lacking room indoors, she converted the barn into a training floor, with ramps, slick patches, and heavy doors that swing back at you. She picks her puppies for indifference to noise rather than for spark, because a fearful animal freezes at the worst possible moment. Having seen firsthand what fear produces, she rejects any method that leans on it. Her former pupils still return regularly to ask for her advice.

units: the new tank of a public aquarium comes under review
the curved panes warp the outlines of the fish
lighting that runs too harsh throws glare off the scales
the fish bunch into one corner of the tank
an artificial current was added to spread the fish out
filters have taken the edge off the lighting
the visitor route stays too narrow near the entrance
the writer calls for that passage to be widened
the installation is judged a success in spite of these flaws
text: The tank that opened in the mild season deserves a hard look before any praise is handed out. Its curved panes flatter from across the hall, but they warp the outlines as soon as you step up close: a tail fin reads far broader there than it truly is. The first lighting ran too harsh, and the scales threw off so much glare that the dark markings along the back simply vanished. The fish, put off by it, bunched into one blind corner and dropped out of sight altogether. The staff answered. An artificial current now spreads them through the whole volume, and tinted filters have taken the edge off the beams. One serious flaw remains, the visitor route, so narrow near the entrance that groups jam up there. It needs widening. Even so, the installation holds up against the best of them.

units: the writer asks a breeder for advice
he cannot settle between two animals to keep at home
the rabbit needs room to run every day
the bird takes long absences without harm
the rabbit gnaws through any cable within reach
the bird keeps up a steady noise that is hard to bear
the writer lives in a cramped home
he asks for an answer before the visit he has planned
text: Madam, I am writing to ask your advice, since your years of breeding will guide me better than the pamphlets I have been reading. I cannot settle between a rabbit and a pet bird, and each case seems to me as strong as the other. The rabbit needs room to run every evening, or else its muscles waste away; the bird takes my long absences without any harm, which counts for a great deal given how often I travel. On the other side of the ledger, a rabbit gnaws through any cable left within its reach, while a bird keeps up a steady whistling that my neighbors are unlikely to forgive. My home is cramped, and no balcony extends it, so that weighs heavily in the balance. Would you be kind enough to write back before the visit I have planned for next week? Please accept, madam, the assurance of my respect.

units: the antlers of deer drop off and build back over each yearly cycle
the horns of cattle and their kin lengthen without ever coming away
antlers are made of plain bone
horns wrap a bony core in a hard sheath
building antlers back demands feed rich in minerals
males settle their rivalries with these appendages
the females of some species carry horns as well
shed antlers are gnawed down by small mammals
text: Walkers ask the same thing over and over again: are antlers and horns one and the same? They are not, and the clearest split between them lies in what becomes of each. A deer's rack drops off once the rut has ended, then builds itself back over the cycle that follows, while the horn of a bull or a goat lengthens without pause and never comes away at all. What are they made of? The first is plain bone, fed during its growth by a covering of velvet skin; the second wraps a bony core in a hard fibrous sheath. Does all that regrowth cost anything? It does, and it demands feed rich in minerals. What good are they? Males settle their rivalries with them, and in some species the females carry horns as well. And afterward? The racks left lying on the ground get gnawed down by voles and squirrels.
